      "text": "The Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act of 1993 (Public Law 103-159), commonly called the Brady Act or Brady Bill, required federal background checks for firearm purchases from licensed dealers and established an interim five-business-day waiting period for handguns.\nIt is named for James Brady, the White House press secretary who was severely wounded and left partially paralyzed in the March 30, 1981, assassination attempt on President Ronald Reagan by John Hinckley Jr. Brady and his wife Sarah led a long public campaign for the measure.\nKey details\n• Sponsor and passage: Introduced in the House by Rep. Charles E. Schumer (D-NY). After years of prior attempts, it passed the House (238-189) and Senate in November 1993. President Bill Clinton signed it into law on November 30, 1993; it took effect on February 28, 1994.\n• Interim provisions (handguns only, until late 1998): Federally licensed dealers, manufacturers, or importers could not transfer a handgun to an unlicensed person without first receiving a statement of eligibility, verifying identity, notifying the chief law enforcement officer in the buyer’s area of residence, and waiting five business days (or less if cleared sooner). Local officials were to make a reasonable effort to check for disqualifying records. Exceptions existed (e.g., certain permits or threats). Records for approved transfers were to be destroyed.\n• National Instant Criminal Background Check System (NICS): The law directed the Attorney General to create a national instant check system within five years so dealers could quickly verify whether a transfer of any firearm would violate federal or state law. NICS (run by the FBI) went online on November 30, 1998, after which the five-day waiting period ended. Dealers contact NICS; if no prohibiting information is found (or after three business days with no response), the transfer can proceed.\n• Other elements: It funded improvements to state criminal records systems, included provisions on multiple handgun purchases (reporting to local police), and contained some reforms related to federal firearms licenses. It applied only to sales by federally licensed dealers (private sales were not covered federally).\nContext and impact\nThe Act built on the Gun Control Act of 1968 by ending the previous “honor system” in which buyers simply certified they were not prohibited persons. Prohibited categories include felons, fugitives, certain domestic violence offenders, illegal aliens, and those adjudicated mentally defective, among others. Background checks have blocked millions of attempted purchases by prohibited persons over the decades.\nA 1997 Supreme Court decision (Printz v. United States) held that the federal government could not compel state/local officials to conduct the interim background checks, but the overall framework and NICS continued.\nThis remains the primary federal law requiring background checks for purchases from licensed firearms dealers.",
